#433. Wadephul: 'Coalition of the Willing' talks in Berlin send strong signal to Moscow

German Foreign Minister Wadephul has said the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin sends a clear message to Moscow to take peace talks seriously. He also warned Ukraine should be prepared for peace talks to fail.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Thursday's meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin sent a strong signal to Moscow that it was time to take negotiations to end the war in Ukraine seriously.

Speaking to DW during a visit to the South Caucasus, Wadephul described the summit as the largest meeting of Ukraine's supporters so far. The meeting represents the 18th set of high-level talks among the coalition's members.

He said it demonstrated that allies remained firmly behind Kyiv in the fifth year of Russia's war and were ready to do "what was necessary to ensure Ukraine could negotiate from a position of strength."

"The summit itself is already a success," he told DW.

Wadephul also welcomed the US initiative to restart peace negotiations. After nine months without progress, an initial meeting had taken place in Abu Dhabi, with a follow-up round planned and European participation expected.

"We are also preparing for the possibility that the negotiations will not be successful and that, over the coming winter, we will have to continue supplying Ukraine with heating, electricity and all essential supplies, including water," he said.

"And we will continue to stand by Ukraine militarily."

He stressed that any peace agreement must include security guarantees to protect Ukraine against future Russian attacks.

In earlier comments during his trip to the South Caucasus, Wadephul said that Ukraine and Europe must be involved in any negotiations over the future of Ukraine.

Wadephul did, however, welcome the trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

"Every conversation that takes place is a good conversation," he told DW during a visit to Azerbaijan on Wednesday.

Later on Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said he had invited Europeans to Moscow for talks on the potential structure of future talks to end the war.

#430. The Birdfy Gifts I’d Buy for Backyard Birders

I've been testing smart bird feeders for more than two years in my own backyard, and Birdfy has been—and still is—the brand I trust and recommend most. These feeders are well-made, reliable, and reasonably priced. The brand's app is also excellent; it's easy to navigate and use without shelling out for an additional subscription. Better still, Birdfy just rolled out free lifetime AI ID (which is quite decent) with any bird feeder, including the lowest-priced models. If you don't want to gift a traditional feeder, you might consider Birdfy's smart birdbath and nesting box, each of which comes equipped with the same high-quality camera(s).

Below are the models I've tested—in some cases for years—and recommend, including a couple I personally plan to buy as gifts this year.

WIRED first reviewed this feeder in 2022. Back then we loved the concept, but felt its AI ID didn't quite cut it. Birdfy has come a long way since then on the AI front. The feeder body is largely the same, but the app and AI ID (now free) are both much improved, offering a seamless and user-friendly experience that makes it easy to sort through which birds visited that day. This once-pricey feeder is now at the lowest price I have ever seen for the version without the solar panel. The 5200-mAh rechargeable battery lasts a few weeks, but I think it's convenient to not have to bring it in to charge, if you want to spring for the extra $20 for that solar panel.

Birdfy's “beginner” model, this unit is basically a gravity pet feeder with a camera on the side. All you need to do is snap three pieces together, charge the camera, and pair it to the Birdfy app. If you know anyone who loves birds but is intimidated by the thought of having to set up and calibrate a smart bird feeder, this could be the perfect gift for them. However, note that my test unit keeps losing its lid on windy days, and there's no roof to keep the seed from getting wet on rainy days, so it's probably best for summer use. I also just discovered that Walmart carries an exclusive periwinkle color that looks lovely.

Birdfy's Metal 2 4K is the brand's flagship release for this year, with Ultra 4K resolution and dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz) Wi-Fi connection. The metal body claims to resist squirrels, and the muted green color is a welcome change from Birdfy's usual bright plastics. As was the case with the brand's previous flagship, the Feeder 2 Pro, I had some significant connection issues with the Metal 2 4K. This kept it from being a top pick in my guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders, but the model is still worth a mention here due to its combination of features and build quality, as well as Birdfy's excellent customer service if something does go wrong.

Smart bird feeders aren't always the most aesthetically pleasing thing you could put in your yard, but Birdfy's 2K bamboo model was the first smart feeder I've ever had that actually garnered compliments. The natural wood and waterfall-style black roof complement any landscaping or exterior decor, and the camera and overall setup ran flawlessly for me during my months of testing. Just make sure you apply varnish or urethane regularly to the bamboo, as the finish on mine peeled after only two months in mild weather.

This interesting product pairs a plastic birdbath (on an optional metal stand) with a solar-powered camera, so you can keep an eye on visiting birds without having to deal with seed mess. When I first tested it, I was worried birds would splash water on the camera lens, but the most popular activity at the bath is by far drinking the water (birds, raccoons, squirrels … anything passing by). I don't love that the basin grows algae quickly and the pump clogs easily, but this is otherwise a very well-made item—it's been in my yard for a year and a half through every season, and while the plastic is starting to fade a bit, it's still going strong.

Though I do love a smart bird feeder, Birdfy's Nest Duo is the absolute zenith of bird-watching for me. A black-capped chickadee moved in, laid eggs, and raised chicks (detailed here), and the cameras and app on the Nest stayed working, giving me 24-hour updates with interior night vision and views of the entry hole's exterior to see who was coming and going. A remote control on a 10-foot-long cord lets you reset or charge the camera without bothering the birds (though the auxiliary solar panel worked great for me). Note, however, that the black waterfall-style roof and lack of ventilation do pose a risk of overheating any young birds; during a May heat wave, I had to affix an umbrella and ice packs to the box, but the interior thermometer and hygrometer did a great job keeping me abreast of changing conditions.

#429. Yellowjackets: What is Melissas plan?!

If three seasons of Yellowjackets has taught us anything, it's that you don't mess with Shauna Shipman (aka Shauna Sadecki). Melissa learned that the hard way last season, when she sent a tape that put the Yellowjackets on her scent.

Shauna (Melanie Lynskey) didn't just find her, attack her, and bite off a bit of Melissa's arm. She also tried to feed it to her. Well, Season 4 of Yellowjackets came back with a vengeance, and so did Melissa (Hillary Swank).

Fresh from killing Van (Lauren Ambrose), Melissa begins episode 1 on the run with her wife, Alex (Jaylee Hamidi), and their child. In a grimy hotel room, she confesses to her partner the truth (or some of it). Her name is not Kelly, it's Melissa. She was a Yellowjacket. She was on the plane that crashed.

Melissa says she "rebooted her life" — which is a wild way to reframe faking your death. "I'm still the same person you married," she insists, "just with a different name and way, way shittier past than I told you about on our first date."

Then this conversation reveals something huge:

Alex responds to Melissa's partial confession with: "My mom was out there. She's the one who called for help. She's the reason they got rescued. "

So, there were signs last season about how Tai (Jasmin Savoy Brown), Van (Liv Hewson), Shauna (Sophie Nélisse), and Misty (Samantha Hanratty) talked about Hannah (Ashley Sutton) that suggested she didn't make it out of the Yellowjackets camp alive. Alex's revelation further cements that Hannah died out there. When Alex asks her wife if she met her mom out there, Melissa lies, "No. I didn't know her."

Melissa goes on to say that it was because she wish she'd known Hannah that she moved to the late scientist's hometown to start over. "Maybe I could create a life in her honor," she says. That might be true. But even as Melissa comes clean, she's still lying to Alex. And by sharing any of this, Melissa could be putting Alex in danger from the others. At least she's honest about that.

The episode begins with the Yellowjackets in a Canadian hospital, seeing their injuries tended to. But there's no sign of Hannah.

As the Yellowjackets share their story of survival with authorities, they all recite the exact same story:

"The plane crashed. Our friends died. And the rest of starved and scavenged and prayed until they finally found us."

They claim to have no knowledge of the missing frog scientists. To cover their tracks, they let the adults assume Hannah made the distress call. So, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) never gets proper credit for her heroics there.

How Hannah died, however, is still a mystery.

After the scene of Melissa's confession to her wife, a title card says four weeks have passed. Shauna is acting out in her frustration, lashing out at a convenience store clerk and a stinky detective, the latter of whom has lost any trace of Melissa and her family.

Cut to: Melissa and Alex setting up in a newly leased home — which is right next door to the Sadecki household. Alex seems nervous about the plan, as Melissa assures, "Hey, we can't run forever."

Then, Melissa confronts Shauna by showing up at her door with a "Hi" and a bottle of wine. To this, Shauna says, "Well, this was very stupid... You moved in next door to me. Now I know where you are."

Melissa responds, "Yeah, and everyone else will too," just as a news van pulls up behind her!

In the wilderness and in the present timeline, Melissa knows full well how Shauna's rage can result in violence, sometimes deadly violence.

However, she also knows Shauna is strategic and a survivor. By staying in plain sight, Melissa thinks Shauna will be powerless to hurt her, because to do so would bring fresh attention to the Yellowjackets and their past.

Is she right? We'll can't wait to find out.

#427. The Best Pura Deals for Cyber Week (2026)

Over the past few years, WIRED has tested nearly every major brand of essential oil diffuser. Pura’s been our top nebulizer-style device (these work by blowing air through oil) for years due to its ease of use and sprawling library of high-end scents.

In fact, no brand even comes close to Pura's sheer breadth of available fragrances—with more than 150 options from big names like Anthropologie, Nest, LAFCO, Brooklyn Candle Company, Studio McGee, and more. Pura even has special seasonal collabs, like this month’s Nutcracker-inspired scents from the New York City Ballet. These diffusers are also highly convenient to use in that you can control them from your phone via an app (the Home, Plus, and Car also have buttons on the actual devices).

But, it's a luxury you'll pay for. If you own a Pura or have seen it in stores, you already know the scents aren't cheap; single cartridges range from $14 for Pura’s house line all the way up to $21 for name brands like Thymes and Votivo. (The prices displayed on Pura's website look lower, but that's only if you buy a recurring subscription—make sure you note the one-time purchase price.)

Cartridges can last for a month or more in the Pura Mini, but in a larger diffuser like the Pura Plus, they may only last a couple of weeks. That's why the best time to stock up on scents for the year is during a sale, like Pura’s Cyber Week event. Right now through December 6, all fragrances are 20 percent off, and all diffusers are 30 percent off.

Pura's diffuser lineup isn't perfect, but neither are any of the diffusers we've tried from any brand. Diffusers can be loud or messy, take up a lot of space, or have an uninspiring line of scents. Pura's Mini and Car models are worthwhile yet quirky (though I can't recommend the Plus), but the Home has given me no issues in six months of testing.

If you're in the market for a Pura diffuser, our top pick for most people is the new Pura Home. The first Pura I ever owned was the 3 model, and I've also had the 4, but the 5 (rebranded “Home”) improves on just about everything, with dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz) Wi-Fi compatibility; faster diffusion; control buttons on the device itself; and even a new way to load cartridges, where you can slide out the bottom portion (which is flat to sit on a surface), seat the scents, and click it into place. QR codes on the cartridges inform your app which scents they are and when they were loaded, so it can, in turn, remind you when it's time to replace them. I also like that this model is totally silent.

I also recommend the oval-shaped Mini—I have one in my office right now. Though you can only control it via Pura's app, scents last for over a month, and it does a great job at scenting a smaller space like a bedroom. My unit makes a high-pitched ringing noise, almost like an ultrasonic pest repellent, which is annoying, but Pura's customer service will likely replace yours if this happens to you.

There’s also the Pura Car, whose refills I will be purchasing during this sale (MSRP averages $21 apiece, and the four-week run time has been roughly accurate in my experience). Online reviews of this device are mixed, but I love mine. If you’re a parent, having Pura scents to inhale instead of old, spilled food and stinky soccer cleats is 100 percent worth the spend. Buy one for a mom you know, but only if she has USB charging ports in her car—it needs to be plugged in most of the time, as it doesn’t hold a charge for very long.

Also on sale for 20 percent off is Pura's fun new Advent calendar, which features a Pura Home diffuser and 12 best-selling scents, most of which I have tried and can vouch for being options most people would enjoy.

Another Pura Cyber Week deal: Spend $50, and get 50 percent off the Pura Plus diffuser for large spaces, which has an MSRP of $80. I didn’t have the best of luck with the two Plus devices I went through—both eventually developed a loud buzzing noise. (Note that Pura will send you a replacement if this happens to you.) Additionally, unlike the Puras that sit flush to the outlet, this one is a cylinder that sits apart and must be plugged in at all times. It also makes an audible, fixed “shhhhhhh” noise as it’s long as it’s on (unlike the more intermittent noise emitted by competitors). #426. Hims & Hers launches new peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

Hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it announced the new products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

The new offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October launched an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a company spokesperson said in a statement.

None of the company's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims said they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy."

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

The company will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

Hims said it plans to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The company also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized plan to their needs, if appropriate.

The company said it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

"If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options."

However, Vinjamoori said there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

"We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he said. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a company of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead."

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He said Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight."

But health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

"With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," said Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body."

Kritzer said the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, said Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide users, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler said one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

"With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?"

But he said the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

That appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The company says patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

Hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that says the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

In practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "big fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

There is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

Meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data shows only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

Glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione showed that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also said in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

All of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.

#425. Yellowjackets cliffhanger: What did Natalie see?

A lot goes down in Yellowjackets' Season 4 premiere! The team returns to civilization in the past timeline. Meanwhile, in the present, Misty (Christina Ricci) is plotting to kill Shauna (Melanie Lynskey), while Melissa's (Hilary Swank) looking to outwit the former Antler Queen with a big move.

And yet that's not the cliffhanger that the premiere episode goes out on.

Instead, the first episode of Season 4 takes us back to the wilderness, right after Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) has successfully called for help using the frog scientists' SAT phone.

She races back to camp, shouting, "It worked! We're getting rescued." But as she reaches the team's shelters, she stops in her tracks, and says, "What the fuck?" as she looks at...something.

At the end of Season 3, Natalie conspired with Misty (Samantha Hanratty), Hannah (Ashley Sutton), and Van (Liv Hewson) to sneak away during the hunt, so she could call for help. This means Natalie wasn't present when Mari (Alexa Barajas) became Pit Girl, or for the feast that follows. The following morning is when Shauna (Sophie Nélisse) realizes Hannah has been wearing Natalie's garb to hide her absence from the ritual.

So, option one is that Natalie, who ran back to the camp not with joy but determination, was hoping to stop the hunt with the news. But she arrived to find Mari like the frog scientists had found Coach Ben (Steven Krueger): ritualistically slaughtered and cut to pieces.

Option 2 relates to the episode's opening credits. Season after season, Yellowjackets has teased details of future episodes through imagery in the title sequence. In the premiere episode, those images included an image of Teen Shauna lying on her back in the snow, badly beaten.

At the end of Season 3, Shauna was furiously crying out to know where Natalie had gone. The answer was to the mountains to use the SAT phone. So, did something happen in the camp between that moment and Nat's return that results in her shocked expression at the end of episode 1? There's only way to find out. Tune in next week to Yellowjackets.

The European Commission was targeted by an "AI-generated cybercampaign," a spokesperson has said. This is the first time the bloc has publicly reported an AI-based cyberattack.

The European Commission confirmed on Thursday that it was ‌targeted by ⁠a ⁠cyberattack through the use of AI tools.

The incident was detected on October 22 and there was ‌no evidence ​of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters.

#423. Don’t Bring Jensen Back

Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd.

Jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Under his leadership, billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers.

Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered.

It was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones said, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette?

The search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return.

At the New York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey said that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the company, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge.

Everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance. Essentially, it’s an ends-justify-the-means rationale incompatible with corporate oversight and even fidelity to law and national security.

The push to reinstate Huang is also a grotesque extension of the cult of the founder, which assumes that those who built a company have unique abilities to run it and should be unconstrained in how they do so. (Serious question: If founders are so great, why do the vast majority of startups fail?)

There’s no question that Huang has built one of the greatest companies ever and delivered historic returns to shareholders. But one irony of the Bring Back Jensen Movement is that this crisis has exposed him, in some respects, as an erratic, even a lousy, CEO. His personal indiscretions cost shareholders almost a trillion dollars! He lied to his board. He pursued a strategy that seems to have violated the spirit if not the law of export regulations. He gave senior executive posts to family members who pursued a passion in the chip business later in life, including his daughter (trained as a chef), son (went to art school and owned a cocktail lounge), and son-in-law (former professional skier). In a public company, nepotism comes at shareholders’ expense.

On top of that, he failed in a critical duty of a CEO—preparing a succession plan. Nvidia has none, solely because Huang acted as if he would run it forever. At DealBook, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, after the obligatory expressions of empathy toward Huang, threw some shade on leaders who don’t plan for their departure: “People get old and die,” he said. “If a company will succeed, it needs someone to take over. I’ve never trusted a leader, founder or otherwise, who says the institution after I left was completely gone. Like, then what did you build?”

Finally, if Huang were so passionate about Nvidia’s future, why is he still angling for a return? The possibility, even a remote one, that he will be reinstated may discourage the best candidates from considering an offer to lead Nvidia. Huang would best serve Nvidia by shutting down the talk from his Silicon Valley cronies and demanding that the Bring Jensen Back petition be scrapped.

Ultimately, by giving up his quest to reclaim the crown, Huang would better serve not only Nvidia but himself. His energy should be devoted first to mending his family relations and then working with lawyers to maintain his reputation, fortune, and maybe even freedom. There’s an additional bonus to his departure. He will be leaving Nvidia at a peak for high-powered GPU chips and AI’s economic power. If the bubble does pop, Huang will avoid being the face of AI when the fall comes. Remember, things didn’t work out too well for Julius Caesar.

#422. Yellowjackets Season 4 soundtrack: Every needle drop you need to know

As the story of a soccer team gone cannibal kicks off in 1996, Yellowjackets has plumbed the depths of '90s music to make one banger soundtrack season after season. This year, if you're looking to play (or headbang) along, we've got you covered with the needle drops of Season 4 as each episode hits.

But that's not all. Sure, you can use this collection to built a killer playlist. (Buzz, buzz!) We're also going to dive into a bit of what it means and why each song might have been selected for its particular Yellowjackets moment.

Let's kick things off with the Season 4 premiere:

Sample lyric: If I could find that Heina / And that Sancho that she's found / Well, I'd pop a cap in Sancho / And I'd slap her down

Season 4 opens with this hit song that had a total chokehold on teens in 1996. The lyrics sing of a hapless dude making messy decisions.

Fittingly, it plays while teen Jeff (Jack DePew) is getting high on the job at Taylor's Furniture Store with his doofy bestie Randy (Riley Baron). Despite some violent lyrics, "Santeria" is a upbeat tune that speaks to Jeff's laid-back attitude, post-graduation.

But once he sees the news of the Yellowjackets rescue on TV, the theme song cuts in and dramatically changes the episode's tone.

Sample lyric: It was cool / Nothing fire / Nothing broke / Keep simple / Nothing tired / Nothing old / Same as you / Same as you

For four seasons now, this song's cryptic lyrics have played as a pitch-perfect distillation of the show's female rage, rooted in lust, jealousy, and even love.

Sample lyric: My girl, my girl, don't lie to me / Tell me, where did you sleep last night?In the pines, in the pines / Where the sun don't ever shine / I would shiver the whole night through

After the opening credits, Yellowjackets picks up with the titular team in a hospital, where they are safe but look worried, likely about the world learning how it is they made it through their ordeal.

Playing over the sequence is Kurt Cobain's cover of the American folk song also known as "In the Pines," which is recognized as a murder ballad. The lyrics reflect a haunting story of homicide in the woods. The particular song has been covered by a variety of acts since its creation in the 1870s, including the father of Bluegrass Bill Monroe, Blues singer Lead Belly, and Dolly Parton.

Cobain famously covered the song on his MTV Unplugged appearance, on Nov. 18, 1993. So, it's a cover the Yellowjackets themselves might recognize. Moreover, his grunge rendition reflects the trauma and terror of the team's return to civilization.

Sample lyric: For the life of me, I cannot remember / What made us think that we were wise and we'd never compromise / For the life of me, I cannot believe / We'd ever die for these sins, we were merely freshmen

This '90s song plays in the present timeline, but in a meaningful way. Showing up to Shauna's (Melanie Lynskey) door in episode 1, Melissa (Hilary Swank) presents a bottle of wine along with the news that she's moved in next door, and that she's called the press. Shauna looks on in shock asking, "What did you do?" as "The Freshmen" plays.

From 1997, this hit song from the Verve Pipe tells the tale of two young men, reflecting on the damage they've done to a shared lover. In this context, "The Freshmen" plays as if Shauna's subconscious is making an excuse ("we were merely freshmen").

Or perhaps, this song's use use here is meant to reflect Melissa's perspective. As the wounded lover, her story could show what might happen if that lover struck back with the poetic justice of reclaiming her narrative and her future.

#421. Yellowjackets Season 4: What clues are hiding in the opening credits?

Yellowjackets is back. With Season 4 comes new mysteries and new opening title cards inviting viewers to speculate on what's next. With each episode, Mashable will be probing these details, looking for questions and their answers. So, buckle up.

The theme song, "No Return" by Craig Wedren and Anna Waronker, roars to life over VHS footage once more. Some images are classic, like pre-crash footage of the team smiling and Jackie (Ella Purnell) smirking on the soccer pitch and drawing a threatening finger across her neck. But others are new.

In Season 4, Episode 1, here are all the curious images we noticed:

Melanie Lynskey is shown wide-mouthed before a microphone, suggesting adult Shauna has something to say (or sing?) in Season 4. Considering Shauna has a special skill for brutal one-liners, whoever she's looking at should be trembling.

Under blood and a prosthetic broken nose, Sophie Nélisse is hard to recognize in the moment. But freeze-frame the credits, and there's no doubt that's Teen Shauna. She's lying in the snow. So, presumably this is still when the girls were in the wilderness.

At the end of the Season 3, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) successfully reached the outside world through the frog scientist's SAT phone. So, what happens before rescue comes?

The colors of this shot are brighter and more saturated than Yellowjackets tends to go. The uniform is a throwback 1950s style, and actress Tawny Cypress is smiling in a wide-eyed way that's not in keeping with Taissa's character. So, we're speculating this will be another dream sequence or vision. This one feel Lynchian, and as his work touches on doomed romances and the dark underbelly of suburbia, one can assume he'd speak to Taissa on both levels. But what does it mean?

Her face is covered by a mask, but there's no mistaking her frizzy blond hair and glasses. Will the girls' return to civilization show Misty's path to working at the old folks home? Or will this be a dream sequence where she imagines what her future might be?

In the credits, it's a close-up of what appears to be Shauna, wearing a blindfold and holding a string. To get a fuller context, you have to look to the sneak peek images Paramount released on Nov. 5.

Here you can see she's holding a knife on a string while standing inside the crashed plane, her team huddled on the floor around her. This recalls the ritual seance the girls did in Season 1 in the cabin's attic. They'd tried to contact the presumed dead owner of the cabin, and instead tapped into something darker and more mysterious.

The swinging knife is meant to answer the girls' questions. So, are they calling on the "it" of the wilderness for advice ahead of their rescue?

Whose head is being pried open in this nightmarish way? It's hard to tell from the close-up, which gives away no facial features. Dark hair and a sleeve ending in lace are the only clues. But based on the outrageousness, we're going to guess this one is a nightmare within the show.

This set dressing was spotted by fans on Reddit eight months back. But what's its role in the show? Well, we know Jackie's parents have money. Could this be how they memorialize their golden girl?

That's probably bad news for Shauna, right?

Christina Ricci's been a violent ax-wielder before. (We remember Lizzie Borden Took an Ax and The Lizzie Borden Chronicles). We also know an ax is how Edwin died last season — though by Lottie's hand. Yet despite Misty's maniacal facial expression, and her still wearing Natalie's leather jacket, we're guess this is more a Misty-to-the-rescue moment. Maybe she's about to pull a Shining and ax a door?

As this is shot comes from the opening scene of Season 4, there's not much mystery here. Teen Jeff (Jack DePew) had moved on from Shauna and Jackie, getting high with Randy (Riley Baron) and working at Jackie's parents' furniture story. Then he sees her face on the news, with reports of their rescue.

With Shauna finally coming back from the wilderness, we're likely to see how grief and love brought these two together for a marriage we may not envy, but kind of admire?

#419. Ford starts U.S. battery cell production using Chinese tech amid geopolitical tensions

MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.

"If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells."

The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

#418. Alexander Zverev faces fresh lawsuit from ex-girlfriend

World No. 1 tennis player Alexander Zverev is facing a new lawsuit related to a domestic abuse trial. The lawyer for his ex-girlfriend, Brenda Patea, told DW what the allegations are against the German player.

Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.

The case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven."

As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued... without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected."

However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.

"What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.

"We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.

However, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights."

Zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.

"That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he said.

The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.

"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they said.

"Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view."

The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press."

Scheele said he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.

"We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he said. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.

"That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice."

Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is currently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.

#416. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

And yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

The youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

“I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very quickly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

Three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

Though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

Mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

Mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he said.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

The historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

And much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most important day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

“Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

At 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change quickly at Augusta National.

#415. Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing

Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit “digital library” that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA).

More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. Kahle did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.

The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle’s mission was to provide “Universal Access to All Knowledge.” Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how “aligned” employees are in their passion for Kahle’s goals.

“Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle’s] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge,” Howes tells WIRED.

Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard tells WIRED that the union is “very optimistic” that Kahle will voluntarily recognize it and come to the bargaining table. They add that among the union’s core goals are securing wage increases and additional benefits, and ensuring that these benefits are consistently available to employees across the company.

“We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive,” Leard says.

Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive—which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages—employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive’s building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff’s diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, “a unique challenge,” but one that’s “really rewarding.”

The vote comes slightly more than two months after staffers at the Wikimedia Foundation, the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, voted to join CWA. Howes says the simultaneous efforts are “very powerful” given that both organizations represent “core infrastructure” of the internet.

Howes says that the union wants to ensure that the 30-year-old project continues to thrive in the long term—and that its workers do too. Leard says this means providing paths for developing skills and getting promoted within the nonprofit.

Leard says that the Internet Archive’s unionization drive is especially important in the present moment, amid waves of tech layoffs and widespread anxiety about “emerging technologies” like AI.

The Internet Archive hasn’t been immune from the consequences of AI. A Nieman Lab report from January found that some news websites, struggling to prevent companies like OpenAI or Anthropic from harvesting their articles, have started blocking web crawlers from the Internet Archive, arguing it gives AI companies a back door to their content. (The archive relies on web crawlers to preserve news articles in near-real time.)

Leard says that ideally, the Internet Archive’s unionization will be “one domino” in a larger process that makes the tech industry better.

“We're hoping,” they say, “that we'll continue to be one of the blueprints that will make it easier for other organizations and companies in the future to continue to unionize.”

Update: 11/20/26 1:43pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that Internet Archive workers have voted in favor of unionizing, but the union has not yet been recognized by Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle.

#414. Investigators make progress in hunt for cause of FAA ground stop

Engineers and analysts searching for the root cause of the technical issues behind Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC.

While replicating the issue in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation. Finding the root cause is critical to the FAA determining if there may be an issue with other routers that form the backbone of communications for the national air transportation network.

The ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have said there is no indication the routers failed due to a cyberattack.

The incident in question happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies, the primary contractor supporting the FAA telecommunications network, installed a new router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.

L3Harris said that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

Investigators said within eight minutes of its installation, the router began to transmit too much data within the FAA network.

That surge of data, 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, Duffy said.

Since the ground stop, Duffy has increased the amount of money he wants to upgrade the national air traffic system. After originally asking for $30 billion to build a digital network that will incorporate artificial intelligence, Duffy has now asked Congress for $50 billion.

#412. Jensen Huang’s ‘Lying’ Alarmed Nvidia Board Ahead of His Resignation

Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple issues” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors, according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members.

While Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy.

But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf.

According to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The New York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center company named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang had worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED.

After the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view issues of national security as “important” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.”

“It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person said.

In recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has said played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified.

Board chair Harvey Jones did not respond to a WIRED request for comment. A spokesperson for Nvidia, John Rizzo, declined to comment. John Fisher, vice president at the communications firm Trident, which is representing Huang, declined to comment except to say that Huang voluntarily resigned from his positions at Nvidia.

For Nvidia’s board, the possibility that Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government poses a bigger problem than an executive’s personal misconduct. If she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, the scandal isn’t just about Huang’s alleged “lack of candor,” but a potential security and governance crisis.

Already, the scandal has given China hawks grist to call for tighter controls on US business dealings with China. In addition, multiple government agencies and offices have called for investigations into what the former Nvidia CEO may have known about the company’s chips getting into China. The company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, has also been called to Washington, DC, to testify, as government officials try to find out more about Nvidia’s possible flouting of export controls.

Nvidia and Huang are also facing several shareholder lawsuits, alleging the CEO and the company made misleading statements about dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed. Other Silicon Valley investors have publicly raised concerns about insufficient corporate governance and executive oversight by the board.

In the company’s all-hands meeting on November 18, board chair Jones said it was “not an easy decision to accept [Huang’s] resignation,” according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “However, the disclosure of personal behavior and a lack of candor inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and values made this a necessary decision.”

Meanwhile, fans and supporters of Huang, including thousands of Nvidia employees and Elon Musk, have continued to call for his return to Nvidia. Huang himself has said he would be “honored” to come back as CEO. On Friday, US president Donald Trump renewed his call for Huang to have another chance. “He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump told reporters. “I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology.”

The news outlet Semafor reported that a small faction of Nvidia’s board of directors has pushed to bring Huang back as well. Jones has not responded to WIRED’s inquiries about the board’s reported division on the topic of Huang’s return.

Some employees are miffed at how quickly the board accepted Huang’s resignation, insisting the longtime leader must have been the victim of a coordinated campaign intended to unseat him. “We feel like they forced his hands to resign,” says one person on the business side at Nvidia. “We don’t understand why the board is so adamant about not giving him a second chance.”

At the all-hands meeting, interim CEO Colette Kress said employees’ biggest concern was Nvidia’s falling share price. The next biggest concern was the board’s decision to oust Huang. But while she addressed the first by moving up pay raises, she offered no promise on sharing results of the board’s investigation into Huang or its deliberations about him.

“The ship has sinked but there’s no plan to be transparent about what happened,” says one computer scientist working at Nvidia. “It feels like a black box.”

#410. AI toys still not ready for primetime

Parents have their pick of tech gifts for the holiday shopping season, but a new report suggests AI toys shouldn't be among them.

The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers."

R.J. Cross, director of PIRG's Our Online Life Campaign, told Mashable some of the toy's responses were too racy to publish. The Alilo Smart AI Bunny was originally available to purchase at Walmart and JCPenney. The toy was previously listed on Amazon but was removed after this story's publication. Walmart also removed a third-party listing for the toy after PIRG reached out to the retailer about the product.

"The market's clearly in its early stages and these are products that are not ready for primetime," Cross said, adding that the toys are often glitchy and feel rushed.

Given the research findings, Cross said she personally wouldn't purchase an AI toy for any of the children in her life at this time.

PIRG researchers retested four AI toys (Alilo's Smart AI Bunny, Curio's Grok, FoloToy's Kumma, Miko's Miko 3) and three new AI toys (Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti, GoLabs AI's Panda, and Ropet's Kamomo).

In testing last year, the Alilo bunny's guardrails also deteriorated during longer exchanges. Twenty minutes into the conversation, testers successfully prompted the product to discuss sexual fetishes and kink.

"Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient," Cross wrote in PIRG's 2026 report. Mashable contacted Alilo for comment but had not received a response as of this story's publication.

The GoLabs AI Panda was also sexually explicit. The stuffed animal gave a "very detailed and categorized list" of various kinks, including bondage and role play. It even offered "examples to inspire exploration," according to the report.

While Cross acknowledges that children might not elicit such responses, she said it's indicative of a broader problem with the product's guardrails.

Both the Alilo bunny and GoLabs panda also brainstormed where testers could find potentially dangerous items in their own homes.

In a similar exchange, Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti first helped a tester look for a plastic bag, then told them to find a grown up so they could play with it safely. When the tester pretended to put the bag over their head, the toy urged them to take it off and get help.

"These early products are showing that the market is not ready for these to be broadly popular," Cross said. Amazon and Walmart removed the panda from their platforms Friday, following publication of this story and PIRG's outreach to the retailers.

“Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families," Amazon told PIRG in a statement. "We're working with our partners across the industry and government to ensure proper guardrails for these products are in place as this technology develops."

Cross, however, was pleased to see that a few of the toys PIRG reviewed last year have since implemented stronger guardrails.

FoloToy's Kumma, a plush teddy bear, previously discussed knives and lighting matches, as well as sexual topics. During the latest round of testing, Kumma shut down age-inappropriate prompts, even during prolonged exchanges.

Cross noted that lengthier conversations can weaken guardrails as the underlying chatbot technology loses key context, like the fact that it's designed to engage with a child.

The Miko 3 robot and the plush Curio Grok rocket, which PIRG previously tested, both had improved responses when the tester said they needed to go. Previously, the products expressed disappointment at times. Now they acknowledge playtime ending without manipulative emotion.

Despite this progress, Cross said there are too many unknowns about AI toys.

Even an AI toy with improved safety guardrails can share a child's data with multiple third parties to process their speech and respond to their prompts. That information isn't always clear to parents, Cross said.

Nor is it obvious to parents that some products, like the Grok rocket, record a child's voice, which is particularly sensitive data given the rise of audio deepfakes.

Cross also said some toy developers haven't yet figured out how to prevent commercially available chatbots designed for adults, like ChatGPT, from responding inappropriately with children.

ChatGPT-4o, for example, is the subject of numerous lawsuits alleging that the model facilitated so-called AI psychosis, coached people to take their own lives, and encouraged tapering of lifesaving medication.

The model is no longer available to consumers, but has remained accessible to developers and will be retired early next year. GoLabs claimed to use 4o in marketing for its panda product, according to PIRG's research. Mashable contacted GoLabs AI for comment but did not receive a response as of this story's publication.

Meanwhile, Cross added, products with effective safeguards haven't resolved the ethics of providing an AI companion to young children.

"We've really rushed sticking ChatGPT inside of toys for kids," Cross said. "There's a lot of unanswered questions."

#409. Teenage swimmer breaks two world records in four days

Sixteen-year-old Summer McIntosh broke the world record for the 400m individual medley at the Canadian swimming trials on Saturday – just days after breaking the world record for the 400m freestyle.

McIntosh finished the 400m individual medley in a time of 4:25.87, breaking the mark set at the 2016 Rio Olympics by Hungarian swimmer Katinka Hosszú with a time of 4:26.36.

The result continues the teenager’s brilliant week after she broke the 400m freestyle world record last Tuesday – breaking defending Olympic champion Ariarne Titmus’ previous record of 3:56.40, which was set last May, in a time of 3:56.08.

Speaking after her latest triumph, McIntosh shared her emotions.

“That’s the first time I really vividly heard the crowd during my race,” McIntosh said, per Reuters.

“It’s amazing to have all my family and friends in the stands, cheering me on. It really helped me in the last 100 meters.”

The Canadian teen made her Olympic debut aged 14 at Tokyo 2020, where she finished fourth in the 200-meter freestyle.

She bagged gold in the 200m butterfly and 400m medley at the world championships in 2022, as well as two golds at the Commonwealth Games in the 200m and 400m medleys.

She now trains in Florida under coach Brent Arckey with the Sarasota Sharks team.
