#267. One of Apple HomeView's best features will have you cooking like a pro

Apple makes cooking a blast with this new tool on its smart display.

As every home chef knows, using a recipe on your phone is a pain. Nothing is less appetizing than trying to unlock your phone and scroll through a 3,000 word preamble to learn when you should take your eggplant parmesan out of the oven. Beyond the inevitable frustrations, the colony of germs teeming over your phone screen make it a hygienic nightmare.

In comes the Apple HomeView, a versatile smart hub that allows you to manage your various apple products hands free. Released on November 13, 2026, the entertainment hub comes with a 7-inch Liquid Retina display and a bounty of Siri AI features. One of its most useful tool is its Start Cooking feature, which provides an easy-to-navigate recipe in Safari on your HomeView screen. Eliminating the need to constantly return to your iPhone when making a rice pilaf, the HomeView's smart feature integrations make your culinary creations easy and enjoyable.

Before diving into how the HomeView can facilitate your next meal, let's cover a quick prerequisite: your phone. Owning an Apple iPhone or iPad is essential to unlocking your HomeView's best features, as you can seamlessly handoff music, Safari searches, calendar reminders and FaceTime conversations to your smart hub. To use your HomeView, update your iPhone's operating system to iOS 27.2 or later.

If you are exploring a new recipe on your iPhone's Safari app, you can easily transfer the webpage to your HomeView screen by holding it up to your device. Alternatively, you can browse directly for recipes using your smart hub's Siri AI functions or with an old-fashioned web search. Once your HomeView detects that a recipe page is pulled up in Safari, it will offer you the option to follow a recipe via an icon of a spoon and recipe card at the bottom righthand corner of your screen. Simply tap this Show Recipe button and your HomeView will enter its cooking mode.

Once converted to Show Recipe mode, your webpage changes into an easy-to-follow recipe guide, with each step separated into a swipeable slide so you can easily understand and track every step. Simply swipe left to navigate to the next step. The ingredients, meanwhile, are broken out into a checkable list.

If you need to set a timer, Apple's HomeView will automatically offer you the opportunity to begin a countdown preset to your recipe's specifications. Simply click the orange highlighted timeframe text when you want the timer to begin. Once clicked, the countdown will appear at the top of your HomeView's screen. Simply click on the countdown to navigate to your timer's screen.

In addition to making your recipes more manageable, the HomeView helps makes your cooking experience more enjoyable. Now you can dance to Frank Sinatra, check your doorbell camera and review your latest text messages all without leaving the kitchen. No more burning your soufflé because you got distracted while shewing a solicitor off your doorstep.

The darling of Apple's Welcome Home event in October, the smart hub currently retails on Apple's website for $299. Also available at your local Apple store, HomeView comes in two versions. The first is a a self standing speaker that comes in four colors. You can also purchase it as a wall mounted device in either SpaceGray or Silver. Notably, wall mounted devices require you to purchase a mount to set them up and may require professional installation.

As it stands, Apple currently offers two mounting options. The first is a the $79.95 hardwired AC mount from Schneider Home. Sleek and cordless, Apple suggests enlisting a professional installer to attach your AC mount. A cheaper, easier option is the Power Mount USB-C Wall Connector. Costing $59.99, this mount can be self-installed. However, it also requires a 20W or more power adapter, which is sold separately. While Apple offers a 40W Dynamic Power Adapter when purchasing a wall-mountable HomeView, you can likely purchase a cheaper adapter from favorite electronics retailer. Apple also plans to offer a hardwired power over ethernet (PoE) mount, enabling a direct internet connection. However, this option is currently not available.

Once purchased, setting up your HomeView is easy. First, prepare your iPhone or iPad by visiting the Settings app, connect to your home WiFi network and update your device. Next make sure you are signed in to the same Apple account you plan on using for your HomeView.

Now, make sure that your home is added to your Home app. Next, plug in your HomeView via its USB-C cable and adapter. Once the Hello screen appears, unlock your iPhone or iPad and hold it up to your HomeView and complete the setup by following the onscreen prompts.

#266. Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private.

Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.

This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

#265. 5 clever things you can still do with an old DVD or CD player

If you don't have discs to play, they can make for clever fodder for DIY projects.

Old tech has a way of hanging around. You might have a drawer of chargers and cables from outdated devices, or a box of your former phones. There could even be a laptop or two tucked away in a closet. In the age of streaming services, you might also have an old CD or DVD player collecting dust somewhere in your home.

Luckily, enterprising folks on the internet have been working on creative ways to repurpose old CD and DVD players, or at least parts of them, and turn them into a variety of projects. These DIY efforts range in their level of difficulty and skill required to produce. But, if you're handy and already comfortable with electronics, you might glean some inspiration and finally give that old DVD or CD player some new life.

Plus, tackling one of these projects might be another way to keep old electronics out of the landfill and cut down on the amount of e-waste you're producing. Here are five clever things you can still do with an old DVD or CD player.

If you're into photography, there's a relatively easy way to turn the lens from an old DVD player into a macro lens you can use on your phone. Macro photography shows small subjects up close, like a bumblebee on a flower. While this particular tutorial might not get you into the pages of National Geographic, it could be a fun way to play around with what you shoot.

YouTuber Raj K Photo shows how to use a screwdriver and adhesive putty to get the job done. It's as simple as prying out the lens, and wrapping a thin coil of putty around the lens to affix it to your phone's camera. The video notes that you have to get pretty close to the subject to get in focus, but the lens is powerful enough to see the cell structure of a layer of onion and the dirt and grooves on a coin.

If you or someone you know is interested in robotics, but isn't exactly ready to join Boston Dynamics, there are more than a few tutorials online that will show you how to use the motors inside a device like a DVD or CD player to build a simple robot. For example, Blackfish, which offers tutorials and templates for projects, has a template for a cardboard robot who can walk around using a DC motor, an on-off switch, a plastic pulley and a battery. While you might have to purchase the pulley, switch and battery, you can find a DC motor inside your CD or DVD player. Blackfish Space has a video, too, that walks you through assembly.

There's also a tutorial from the YouTube account GrandadIsAnOldMan, which shows how to take the drive from a DVD player and create what he calls an Inchworm CrawlerBot. Essentially, the CrawlerBot uses the motion of the tray opening and closing, driven by its motors, to move itself while on wheels. This project requires a few more parts than the walking robot project, like four VHS cassette spools (in case you're old enough to have those lying around, too), barbecue skewers, a toggle switch, a hot glue gun and a soldering iron, to name a few. He also links to two other iterations of the CrawlerBot.

On the more complicated end of the DIY spectrum, you can use old CD and DVD players to make your own CNC laser engraver of varying sizes. A CNC laser engraver is a machine that can etch, carve or mill on a hard surface like wood, metal or glass, using digital instructions. You might use this method to put a custom image or text on something.

In particular, Autodesk Instructables features YouTuber How To Do's 8-step guide to making one such CNC laser engraver, which uses two optical drives from either a CD or DVD player, as well as an Arduino board, which is an "open-source electronics platform" that will serve as the "brain" of the machine, according to the instructions. In the video description on YouTube, you can see a list of materials with links. Since the video is about 9 years old, not all the links might work. You also might note that the creator uses more than a few shop tools. He says that in reality, if you want a CNC laser engraver, you can just buy one — it'll be cheaper and easier. But undertaking this project is, as they say, about the journey.

If you're looking to hide some personal items from prying eyes, you can turn a DVD or CD drive into a motorized drawer. Kipkay on YouTube offers a video on how to do it. You'll need a drive, a 3-volt button cell battery and holder, a magnetic switch (Kipkay mentions getting one from an old alarm system), a strong neodymium magnet, a small wire, and some type of glue.

Part of the process involves removing the guts of the drive. Along the way, you can save some components like the laser diode for other projects. Ultimately, the magnet is what will trigger the switch, opening your new secret stash drawer. The drawer can even be attached somewhere like under a desk. You won't be storing large items, but Kipkay suggests there's room for things like cash and SD cards. You can also read the directions on Instructables.

Even if you don't have a specific project in mind, you can still take apart an old CD or DVD player and harvest useful parts to use in the future. Instructables, once again, comes through with directions describing what you can salvage and how, via the YouTube account Prajjwal Nag. The instructions note that aside from saving money on parts, the act of disassembling can help you learn how the electronics work.

Among the parts you can reuse from these older devices are DC motors, stepper motors, buttons, LED lights, laser diodes, neodymium magnets, and optical lenses. To retrieve all those bits, you'll need a screwdriver, tweezers, needle-nose pliers, wire cutters and rubber gloves. Instructables also links to projects using some of those parts if you're looking for inspiration.

So, if you're wanting something to do with old CD or DVD players that doesn't just involve throwing them out, (and maybe have a quiet Saturday afternoon) you've got options for turning your old tech into something new and useful.

#264. Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation

Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.

Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.

Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.

On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.

Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album.

Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.

"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.

Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method."

Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.

Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.

"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us."

In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.

"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".

For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.

There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.

Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.

Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with  her colleagues focused largely on science:  "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison."

"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.

Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.

Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.

Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.

The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person."

#263. Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers

Meta is “re-evaluating” 2030 sustainability goals. Will others follow?

Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”

It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

#262. How to set up surround sound with Apple TV 4K and HomePods

Surround yourself with Apple’s premium home theater experience — for a price.

The new Apple TV 4K (4th generation) has been generating buzz ever since it was announced at the Cupertino company's Welcome Home Event in October 2026. One of the most noteworthy changes is to its surround sound capabilities, in which users can create an immersive cinematic experience in their own living room. Unfortunately, while many of the 4th generation's new features will be available for previous models, including its enhanced Siri AI system, Apple's venture into surround sound is not backwards compatible.

To set up your home theater's surround sound system, you will need the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K and up to four 2nd generation HomePods or HomePod mini 2s. Apple's support page also states that you can pair two sets of either home speaker, but the front pair and rear pair must match (two HomePods and two HomePod mini 2s). Before setting up your system, update your devices to the most recent software. If you only have two speakers, either the HomePod or HomePod mini 2, you can still use them to create a home stereo setup.

Those wanting to create this home theater setup from scratch will have to pay a pretty penny to do so. Officially released on November 13, 2026, you can purchase the 4th generation Apple TV 4K on Apple's website or at your local Apple Store for a hefty $299. But true sticker shock may set in when one considers the cost of four smart speakers, with the HomePod (2nd generation) and HomePod mini 2 costing $349 and $149, respectively. All told, that could cost you up to $1,700 for Apple's most advanced audio experience. Whether the system's various AI and quality updates help soften the blow is up to you.

The first thing you should do is assign your Apple TV 4K and HomePod speakers to the same room in the Home app. To assign your Apple TV 4K to a room, turn on your Apple TV and open the Settings app. Next, select AirPlay and Apple Home, navigate to the Select a Room option beneath Apple Home and assign your Apple TV accordingly.

Next, you need to assign your speaker system. To add your HomePod (2nd generation) or HomePod mini 2, turn on your speaker and open the Home app on your iPhone or iPad. Tap the Add button and select Add Accessory. You will be prompted to scan a code or hold your device near the speaker. When it appears, tap the speaker name and tap Allow when prompted to Add Accessory to Network. Finally, choose the same room as your Apple TV 4K, name it, tap Continue > Done. Repeat this process for all four speakers.

You can change the room of an existing HomePod in the Home app on your iPhone or iPad. Simply open the Home application and hold your finger down on the HomePod whose location you would like to change. Next, select the Accessories Settings button with the gear symbol. Press the Room tab and select the room of your home theater. You can also add a new room in this page by tapping Create New. Once you have added all your devices to the same room, you are ready to set up surround sound.

Now, it's time to set up your surround sound configuration. Go to your Home app, tap a HomePod and select the gear icon at the bottom. Then, scroll until you find the Create Home Theater option and tap the HomePods that you want to group into your home theater system. Once grouped, tap the checkmark at the top corner. You should now see a notification instructing you to continue the set up process on your Apple TV.

Next, turn on your Apple TV. Follow the onscreen prompts instructing you on where to place your speakers. If using a combination of HomePods and HomPod mini 2 speakers, Apple suggests that you place the larger speakers at the front of the room. Once in place, select Start Tuning. Your home theater will now begin tuning to your space by playing a series of tones. Once finished, follow the on screen instructions confirming your speaker's placements and color selections before hitting Confirm. Now you are ready for an immersive home theater experience.

If you'd rather create a stereo system using two Apple smart speakers, visit to your Home app, select your HomePod, and tap Settings. Next, tap Create Stereo Pair and follow the onscreen instructions. From there, follow the steps above to assign your stereo to the same room as your Apple TV 4K. Once finished, turn your Apple TV on and follow the onscreen prompts until you are prompted to Use as TV Speakers.

#261. This retro classic is the most re-released game of all time — here's why

The most re-released game is also one of the best-selling, and it’s not even close.

You might initially think the most re-released game of all time is something like Skyrim, which is notorious for its various editions. Or you may instead point to the original Super Mario Bros., which has appeared on almost every Nintendo console in some form, or Sonic the Hedgehog for its inclusion in tons of compilations.

But another classic game dwarfs the appearances of any other: Tetris. Following its initial development on a Soviet computer, this renowned puzzler quickly spread around the world and appeared on virtually every platform you can imagine. With over 200 official releases, alongside countless ports and bootleg versions, there's been a version of Tetris to play no matter what device you have around.

As you may know, the legacy of Tetris started in the Soviet Union in 1984-1985, when programmer Alexey Pajitnov developed games for fun. He first built the game for the Soviet Elektronika 60 computer, using text-based graphics ([] characters for the tetrominoes) since that machine didn't have graphical output.

After its inception, Pajitnov and a few colleagues worked to port the game to the incredibly popular IBM PC before making it known around the region by passing out copies. Pajitnov's manager liked the game and was one of the first who worked to distribute it to other parts of the world. In the following years, versions were created for popular computers at the time, such as the Commodore 64, Amiga and Mac.

Arguably the most important version of Tetris was its release on Game Boy in 1989. Nintendo executives went through a long process, including a legal battle, to license the game for its upcoming handheld. They were ultimately successful in securing the rights, which led to Tetris coming bundled with the console in every market except Japan. This release was the first to have the iconic "Theme A" music; Pajitnov has said it's his favorite version, and it's by far the best-seller (not including mobile versions) with more than 35 million copies sold.

In 1996, Alexey Pajitnov created The Tetris Company with longtime business partner Henk Rogers (who played a huge part in spreading Tetris around the world) to manage future branding and licensing. Since then, the game has been modified, re-released and ported (officially and unofficially) like crazy. There was even a Tetris movie on Apple TV, released in 2023.

Anyone who has played Tetris in any form will understand how addictive its gameplay is. The concept of clearing horizontal lines only takes a moment to understand, and then you can spend a lifetime getting better at it. You only need a few buttons to move and rotate blocks, which, combined with the simple graphics, means Tetris can appear on almost any device, including unofficial ports to unexpected platforms like graphing calculators. Its bundling with the wildly successful Game Boy meant tons of people were exposed to it early on and thus have nostalgia for the game.

As we saw with the various releases above, Tetris also hasn't been stagnant. The Tetris Company has internal rules known as the Tetris Guideline, which dictate how official releases should play, look and be controlled.

Tetris's popularity has even led to other puzzle games using the name for marketing. The SNES game known as Tetris Attack was called Panel de Pon in its original Japanese release, but Nintendo licensed the Tetris name for other markets, assuming people would associate the title with block games in general. Nintendo used the name Puzzle League for later releases outside Japan.

Many people consider Tetris to be a perfect game; its enduring legacy and "easy to learn, tough to master" gameplay definitely put it in the running for one of the best ever.

It's not feasible to discuss every version of Tetris, but it's interesting to look at some of the most notable iterations. The NES release, which also debuted in 1989, is unique because it wasn't intended to be played indefinitely like most other versions. Instead, the game speeds up drastically past a certain point, which was designed to be a run's natural ending. This initially led to competition centering around racking up a max score before the "kill screen," but in recent years, players have developed techniques to play past the point that was previously thought impossible.

NES Tetris also makes for a good competition version because it's more "hardcore." It lacks quality-of-life features present in later releases, like holding a piece, plus there's no grace period for movement once a tetromino touches the bottom — it's locked in instantly. And unlike later games that have a pseudo-random system to make sure you get each tetromino shape every so often, NES Tetris can have droughts where you never see the I-block you need.

The Game Boy Color got Tetris DX in 1998, which updated the Game Boy release with color. It was the first version to offer the now-staple Sprint mode, where you race to clear 40 lines instead of the typical endless gameplay. The New Tetris, released on Nintendo 64 in 1999, was the first mainstream version to allow four players to compete simultaneously. It also marked the introduction of the ability to hold a piece to swap in later.

Tetris DS (2006) is beloved for featuring multiple modes, each themed in the style of Nintendo franchises like Zelda and Metroid. It's regularly cited as one of the best releases and was the first official Tetris game to feature online play.

Skipping forward a bit, Puyo Puyo Tetris is a fun mix of two classic puzzle series. Puyo Puyo is big in Japan but rarely received releases in other regions before this, with most of them being reskins under other franchises like Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine and Kirby's Avalanche. After its Japanese release in 2014, Puyo Puyo Tetris arrived in other regions in early 2017, with various modes that mash up the two play styles.

2018's Tetris Effect is the most beautiful version of the concept. It takes you on a "journey" through various visual landscapes, with lovely background music to immerse you in the experience. You also have the ability to stop time and clear more than four lines at once. It was initially limited to VR platforms, but an expanded version called Tetris Effect: Connected brought it to all modern systems in standard view. Meanwhile, in 2019, Tetris 99 adapted the battle royale craze to the puzzle game, pitting you against 98 people and rewarding you for knocking others out by sending garbage to their boards.

Most recently, 2024's Tetris Forever serves as an interactive museum of the series after 40 years, including interviews and various playable versions.

#260. Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button

Google search is making it even easier to access AI tools on the search page.

Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

The other big change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”

It’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s new AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that shows that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

This change says more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users. As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts. In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction.

#258. HomeView vs. Echo Show: What's the difference between Apple's and Amazon's smart displays?

Both put an AI assistant in your home, but they work in different ways.

Amazon and Google have long been the top choices when it comes to smart displays, but Apple has now joined the race with HomeView. For $299, Apple offers a touchscreen and built-in speakers with an experience optimized for those deeply immersed in the company's ecosystem — it includes Messages, Apple Music and, of course, built-in HomeKit. It's impossible not to compare it to Amazon's Echo Show, which recently added a new 16-inch model to its lineup. But even though both are smart displays, they work in very different ways — and choosing between them ultimately comes down to which ecosystem you have at home.

The differences start with size: While the HomeView is a new product and is available in a single version with a 7-inch square screen, Amazon offers a range of Echo Show devices with different screen sizes. The entry-level Echo Show has a 5.5-inch screen and costs $99 — but if you want to go bigger, there's even an Echo Show with a massive 21-inch screen for $499. They all share mostly the same features, although the 16-inch and 21-inch models can run Fire TV apps.

Amazon's Echo Show 8 is the one that can be easily compared to HomeView, with an 8.7-inch display. The aspect ratio is different, though, as Echo devices have widescreen displays and are better for watching 16:9 videos. The HomeView's square shape might annoy those planning to buy one to watch videos on it. Also on Apple's side, HomeView runs on the same A18 chip as the iPhone 16 — which probably makes it the most powerful smart display available. Amazon, on the other hand, makes custom chips for its Echo devices that aren't exactly designed to deliver Earth-shattering performance.

Both the HomeView and the Echo Show 8 have a built-in camera, but the software makes them work quite differently. The HomeView's 12-megapixel camera only works with FaceTime and a Mirror feature, and, of course, for facial recognition. With the Echo Show 8, you can take selfies with its 13-megapixel camera it or use it as a live-view camera to monitor your home. The sound specs are quite similar between the two of them, as both have two full-range drivers and a woofer. The HomeView's base also packs two passive radiators for a bit more low end.

The biggest difference between the HomeView and Amazon devices is how they work. While the Echo Show is a standalone device linked to an Amazon account that can run directly on your network, the HomeView requires an iPhone or iPad to work — you can't set it up without one. On Echo Show devices, you can also use Alexa+ through your Prime membership to manage calendars, reminders and shopping without your phone. The HomeView comes with Siri AI built-in, but it can only handle personal requests if you have a recently unlocked iPhone 15 Pro or later paired with it and nearby.

Both the Echo Show and HomeView devices can have multiple profiles verified by voice and facial recognition. However, while Amazon lets users manually switch between profiles by asking Alexa, for example, HomeView does it all automatically — which, according to some early reviews, doesn't always work.

The truth is, both products target different users. Amazon treats the Echo Show as a standalone product that fits almost everyone. The HomeView is a different story — it's much more like an accessory for people who already own other Apple products and rely on the company's core apps and features.

#257. US judge approves Bayer's $7.25 billion cancer settlement

Bayer could end years of costly lawsuits in the US over claims that its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer. Tens of thousands of people could now receive compensation, although some lawyers say the payments are too low.

A US judge on Friday approved German chemical giant Bayer's $7.25 billion (€6.60 billion) settlement of lawsuits claiming its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer.

Judge Timothy Boyer in the US state of Missouri ruled that the agreement was "fair, reasonable, and adequate."

The decision could help Bayer end years of costly legal battles over Roundup, which the company acquired when it bought US weedkiller producer Monsanto in 2018.

"The court's final approval is a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation," Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said.

The agreement covers tens of thousands of people who say they developed non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, after using Roundup.

It also covers people who may be diagnosed with the disease in the future after previous exposure to the weedkiller.

Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion into a special fund over the next 21 years.

Individual payments are expected to average between $10,000 and $165,000. The amount will depend on factors including the patient's age, the severity of the illness and how long they were exposed to Roundup.

Some lawyers representing cancer patients have criticized the payments as too low.

But the judge rejected their objections, saying that further delays could leave seriously ill patients waiting years for compensation.

Christopher Seeger, a lawyer representing cancer patients, welcomed the decision.

"Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," he said.

The settlement follows a major victory for Bayer at the US Supreme Court in June.

The court ruled that Bayer could not be sued under state laws for failing to put cancer warnings on Roundup packaging.

The judges argued that US federal rules did not require such warnings and that individual states could not impose additional labeling requirements.

The decision made it much harder for cancer patients to win lawsuits against Bayer.

In October, a Missouri jury also ruled in Bayer's favor in a separate Roundup cancer case.

However, some legal battles continue. Around 200 cases are still being fought in federal courts outside the new settlement, according to Bayer.

Monsanto introduced Roundup in 1974. Its main ingredient, glyphosate, became one of the world's most widely used weedkillers.

Farmers use Roundup to kill weeds without damaging crops that have been genetically modified to survive the chemical. It has also been widely used in private gardens and on lawns.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bayer inherited the legal problems surrounding Roundup when it bought Monsanto for $63 billion in 2018.

Since then, around 200,000 claims have been made against Bayer by people who believe the weedkiller caused their cancer.

The company already agreed to a $10.9 billion settlement in 2020. However, it failed to secure approval for a separate agreement covering future cases.

Some lawsuits have resulted in huge payouts, including a $2.1 billion award to plaintiffs in Georgia.

Bayer has already set aside $16 billion for Roundup-related legal costs. Its shares have fallen by 46% since the Monsanto takeover.

The company has also removed glyphosate from newer versions of Roundup sold to private consumers in the United States.

Scientists and regulators disagree about whether glyphosate causes cancer.

In 2015, the World Health Organization's cancer research agency classified the chemical as "probably carcinogenic" to humans.

However, the US Environmental Protection Agency says glyphosate is unlikely to cause cancer when used as directed.

Bayer has repeatedly denied that Roundup causes cancer, pointing to scientific studies and regulatory approvals.

The debate intensified last year when a major scientific study that had supported Roundup's safety for decades was withdrawn.

The journal that published it cited serious problems, including missing cancer research and previously undisclosed involvement by Monsanto employees.

The withdrawal raised further questions about the influence of chemical companies on scientific research.

#256. SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business

“Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026.”

The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.

“SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.

CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.

SpaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.

During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

On October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

The central question is who decided to curtail the performance of Starshield assets in Ukraine. Accounts have variously implicated Musk, SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the White House. Musk has said that US officials control Starshield access, while defending SpaceX’s right to restrict the use of commercial Starlink service in war.

“My ask to you is straightforward,” Himes wrote to Musk. “Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether those changes were made unilaterally by SpaceX or were directed by a U.S. Government official.”

The communications from Himes suggest that Congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate in January following decisive victories in the Midterm elections, are prepared to not just investigate the disruption of these SpaceX services in Ukraine, but to take action that could threaten SpaceX’s broader national security business.

“It is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems, until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes wrote in his letter to Musk.

Various options are open to Congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans who have raised similar concerns, including demanding classified briefings and documents and restricting funding through appropriations to the US Department of Defense and other federal departments. Notably, the US Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion contract earlier this year to develop the Space Data Network Backbone intended to support the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. That program, along with SpaceX’s work building intelligence satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office, could become a focus of congressional scrutiny.

It seems unlikely that the US government would sever ties with SpaceX for space-based data services or launches, as the company is currently providing capabilities that no other US company can match. But Democrats are clearly serious about putting restrictions on Musk’s ability to influence geopolitical conflicts that have traditionally been the purview of governments rather than corporations.

#255. Setting up an Apple HomeView is ridiculously easy thanks to your iPhone

You can also easily add other users to your HomeView display.

Apple HomeView has arrived, and to set up the smart display, you'll have to use your iPhone or iPad. Unlike other companies' smart displays, the HomeView doesn't run its own apps; it merely mirrors the compatible ones you have on your phone or tablet. It's similar to CarPlay in that regard.

The good news is that pairing it with an iPhone or an iPad is fairly easy. To start with, your iPhone must be running the recently released iOS 27.2, while your iPad must be running iPadOS 27.2. In addition, to be able to make the most of HomeView, you'll have to be comfortable running Apple Intelligence. It's always listening to your Siri queries, and you'll need to use Siri AI, the next-generation version of the assistant powered by Apple Intelligence, to get more useful and conversational responses.

The process of pairing and iPhone or iPad to a HomeView device is simple. You just have to hold your phone or tablet near the smart display that's powered on. You'll then see a card pop up, similar to a new set of AirPods or other Apple devices. If you're not running the latest iOS or iPadOS software, you'll be prompted to update. Follow the on-screen directions (more on those below) and you're good to go.

If you don't see a card, or if you close it accidentally, there is a more manual setup method for the HomeView. After you update your operating system, open the Home app on your phone or tablet. If you've never used it before, you have to set up a new Home. Tap the + icon at the top-right corner of the screen, then Add New Home and give it a name. You will automatically be listed as the Home's Resident (Owner). If you already have a Home set up, tap the ellipsis icon at the top right, choose a Home and make sure you're its Resident (Owner).

Next, open the Find My app and then make sure Shared From is set to This iPhone or This iPad. If it's not set to that option, and you see Use This [device] as My Location, tap it. Check that your phone's Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are switched on. If you haven't powered on your HomeView yet, do it now. Unlock your iPhone or iPad and place it near the HomeView to see a Set Up screen appear on your device.

Now, it's time to pair your devices. You'll see a prompt on your iPhone or iPad, asking you to Center HomeView in the camera frame to capture the animation on the bigger screen. You can also tap on Enter Passcode Manually to get HomeView to show you a four-digit passcode instead. After the frame in the setup screen turns green, the process begins.

You will be asked which Home to add the HomeView to. After you've chosen, you'll get to the Where will you use this HomeView screen, where you'll have to choose the room where you want to add it to. Take note that you may be asked to update the HomeView software. After the update is done, you'll go through more prompts, including one that asks if you want your HomeView to match your iPhone settings, like your Wi-Fi network and Siri voice. Another prompt asks if you want the HomeView to be able to show personal content like messages. Once you're done, the display will show an animation while it's undergoing configuration.

From here, the setup process will move to the HomeView itself. You'll be asked to set up Face and Voice Recognition for a more personalized experience. Remember that you can't display messages and other personal information on the HomeView without authenticating your identity. Tap Continue and follow the instructions.

To set up Voice Recognition, you'll have to read several prompts shown on screen out loud. Next, you'll be able to set Facial Recognition by positioning your face in the center of the camera frame and moving it, according to the instructions on screen. This process is similar to setting up Face ID on other Apple devices. The HomeView will then show you a short tutorial of its features. The moment the Welcome screen appears, you know you're done.

Apple's HomeView supports up to six users on a single device, and you — or the user listed as Resident (Owner) of the Home it has been linked to — can add them after setup is done. Open the Home app and choose the Home linked to your device. Tap the + icon and choose Add People. When asked to choose their Role, choose Resident so they can access the HomeView anytime. You will then be asked to enter their Apple/iCloud account contact and then send them an invite. They can accept the invitation in the More section that shows up when you tap the ellipsis icon at the top right corner of the Home app.

After a user has been added, they can swipe up on the HomeView to access the Home Screen and then tap the profile icon at the top right to choose their account. Once the user brings their iPhone or iPad near the HomeView, a prompt with a Join button appear on their device. They will also have to go through several prompts, including the one asking them if they want the display to match their iPhone settings and whether they want it to show any personal information. They will then officially be added as a user and will be able to set up Voice and Facial Recognition. One user only has to swipe down the Home Screen to exit, and another user can take over once they step in front of the HomeView.

#254. Harbinger is building the unsexy EVs that keep the economy moving

While legacy automakers tap the brakes on electric vehicles, one startup is hitting the accelerator. Earlier this month, electric truck maker Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D round, capping a banner stretch that includes a $300 million order from FedEx and a new defense contract with the US military.

Harbinger is stacking up wins by skipping the consumer EV hype cycle altogether and focusing on the unglamorous workhorses that keep the economy running: Class 4–6 delivery vans and box trucks. The company’s thesis is simple: go after the overlooked commercial segments where legacy trucks are weak and giant automakers can’t be bothered to compete, CEO John Harris tells me.

“We’re not solving the big obvious problem because everyone’s going to solve that problem, and as a result, the margins get kind of ground down to zero,” Harris says. “We’re solving problems that — they’ve just been there forever and you no longer think of this as a problem, you just think of it as like part of existence. It’s like a tax on your life.”

Founded in 2021 by veterans of Canoo, QuantumScape, and Faraday Future, Harbinger aims to fill a structural gap in the auto market, in which most passenger EV platforms lack the durability to scale up while the heavy-duty platforms are too heavy and expensive to scale down.

“In auto, you have Class 1 companies and you have Class 8 companies,” Harris says. “And everything in between is kind of a wasteland... It is much, much, much too small for a big company to serve.”

Which is not to say the industry hasn’t tried. Ford and GM both took shots at electrifying the medium-duty segment with the E-Transit and BrightDrop delivery vans, respectively, but sluggish sales and the loss of federal incentives forced them to discontinue or cancel those models.

Harris says that big automakers are ill-suited to task, with their over-reliance on third-party suppliers to build all the necessary components. The effort becomes too spread out and expensive, with not enough return on your investment. That’s why Harbinger is attempting a more vertically integrated approach, he says, assembling its own battery packs and drive units in house — with inverters to follow.

“If you are not vertically integrated in auto, you don’t build viable products,” Harris says. “We believe that electric vehicles are only viable when they’re competitive on acquisition price with combustion vehicles.”

Of course, Harris and his fellow cofounders have tasted failure in their previous ventures. Harbinger’s CTO Phillip Weicker cofounded EV startup Canoo, which ran out of cash and filed bankruptcy in 2025. Harris himself spent a year at tumultuous Chinese EV company Faraday Future before moving on to Xos Trucks and then Palmer Luckey’s Anduril.

“I was an engineer at Faraday. I wasn’t in charge of anything,” Harris says. “So it’s not like, ‘John, why did Faraday not succeed?’ I can tell you lots of reasons, but it wasn’t because the plastic part that I designed didn’t work. It was because the plastic part that I designed was going into a vehicle for which the world customer base was like three people.”

Those companies “fundamentally didn’t work,” he adds, “because of the market fit issue and the leadership issue. Not because the engineering didn’t work or electrification wasn’t ready or they didn’t have enough capital.”

Harbinger’s approach is more pragmatic, offering both battery-electric and plug-in hybrid powertrains for its medium-duty trucks. The company is not pursuing heavy-duty Class 8 trucks like the Tesla Semi, however, as Harris argues the economics of electric long-haul trucking are unworkable.

“Class 8 electrification to me is one of those markets. I completely reject the notion that that’s a good fit for electrification for the majority of the market,” he says. “We can put [the Tesla Semi] on the watch list with the Cybertruck.”

With companies like Amazon and FedEx making serious moves to secure more electric delivery vehicles, Harbinger is well-positioned to be a key supplier. And with diesel prices skyrocketing as a result of the war with Iran, more companies are waking up to a reality in which EVs can help bring down their costs.

Harbinger isn’t just building delivery trucks — it’s also branching into energy storage and military technology. For example, the company supplies battery power systems to Airstream and partners with American Rheinmetall and Forterra to build self-driving hybrid supply vehicles for the US Army. Harbinger also recently bought Phantom AI to bring advanced driver-assistance features to commercial fleets, in the hopes of giving companies a clear, measurable return on their safety investments.

With millions in fresh capital and major contracts already on the books, Harbinger has cleared the first major hurdle that tripped up its founders’ past ventures. Now comes the hardest part in the auto business: proving it can actually build them at scale.

“Auto is a big enough opportunity that it can get people’s attention,” Harris says. “It’s also punishingly difficult. So if you can make something that works in auto, it will be phenomenal in every other segment, because every other segment, the competition is essentially weaker.”

#253. How much can you get for your old, discontinued Apple Watch?

Your old Apple Watch might still be worth some cash when you trade it in for a new one.

The Apple Watch has become a must-have device for many people, and it can last for years. Chances are that you'll probably buy a new watch before your current one stops working. Still, your old Apple Watch will eventually stop getting software updates — that's what happened this year with watchOS 27, which dropped support for models older than the Series 9. Some of them still get security patches, but the latest features are exclusive to newer devices.

That might make you wonder what you should do with an old, discontinued Apple Watch that you no longer use. Even if you have a legacy Apple Watch, you can resell it or use it for trade-in credit at Apple. They aren't worth much, but it's better than leaving them unused in a drawer to gather dust.

If you don't want to deal with the hassle of selling your old Apple Watch on your own, the Apple Trade In program is the easiest path. With this, you give your used Apple Watch to Apple and you get credit toward a new product in return — that could be another Apple Watch or anything else, like AirPods or even an iPhone.

Apple regularly updates its trade-in pricing table; at the time of writing, you can get as much as $430 in credit for an Apple Watch. The credit amount depends on the model you have and its condition, like whether it's in good shape or has scratches and cracks. If your Apple Watch is an especially old model or badly damaged, Apple won't offer trade-in credit for it, but it still offers free recycling.

Trade-in values start at up to $30 for the first-generation Apple Watch SE, which came out in 2020. An Apple Watch Series 8 is worth $90 max, while a Series 11 is worth up to $200. The Ultra offers the highest trade-in value: Apple pays up to $430 for a used Apple Watch Ultra 3 in good condition. So for example, if you have a Series 8 in good condition and trade it in for a new Apple Watch Series 12 (which starts at $399), the price drops to $309 instead.

Keep in mind that Apple doesn't pay cash for trade-in products. If you don't plan on buying a new product right away, or want the credit for something else, you can receive the value as an Apple gift card instead. It's thus a good way to cover the cost of apps or subscriptions.

You can bring your old watch to an Apple Store or mail it in — all shipping costs are covered. Apple adds your trade-in credit to your account balance as soon as it receives your watch and confirms that everything is in order.

Selling an old Apple Watch on your own takes more effort, but also pays you more. On Swappa, a marketplace for used tech, a Series 6 can be worth around $100 — more than double the $45 Apple offers for it. The same applies to other models, like the Series 8, which is worth around $130.

The amount you can get will depend on which device you have and its condition. Apple Watch models with cellular connectivity and more premium materials, such as steel or titanium, tend to hold their value better than GPS-only and aluminum ones. Just remember to unpair and reset your Apple Watch before trading it in or selling it. Otherwise, Activation Lock will remain enabled, and the buyer won't be able to unlock it without your Apple Account and password. Apple refuses devices with Activation Lock enabled.

And if you decide to keep your old Apple Watch after all, there are some interesting ways to put an older smartwatch to good use, like turning it into your sleep tracker while your main watch charges overnight.

#252. Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules

FCC preempts state rules that require AT&T to keep offering home phone service.

The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.

AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.

The order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.

The FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.

“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”

If AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.

“The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr said.

California says its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against the order, saying that state telecom commissions “are often the last line of defense for consumers. They know their communities, they take their complaints, and they answer to the people who rely on these services in a way that a federal agency in Washington cannot always match.”

Gomez said the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has an open proceeding on how to modernize its COLR rules, and that the FCC should let that process play out. Large technology transitions work best “when the state regulator is a partner with a real role,” but the FCC is treating the CPUC “as an obstacle to be cleared,” she said.

The CPUC “proceeding is the right place for California to weigh what a modern basic service requirement should look like, with input from the people who will actually be making that switch,” Gomez said. “AT&T has said it does not plan to discontinue service before June 1, 2027, which leaves time for the CPUC to finish its work. Rather than wait, this item tells the CPUC to write its new consumer protections around a federal ruling it opposed.”

In March, the FCC issued an order that made it easier for carriers to discontinue copper networks. The order asserted that state rules are subject to preemption if they conflict with the FCC’s discontinuance authorizations and authority. AT&T cited the order in its lawsuit against California.

Trump officials and telecom companies have been trying to block California’s rules for years. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws throughout the country in 2019, and California later defeated ISPs in a lawsuit that challenged its net neutrality law in court.

California’s net neutrality law and other telecom regulations are again being threatened by rules the Trump administration applied to federal grants, but California rejected US demands to stop enforcing its laws this month. In that case, California may have to choose between enforcing its telecom laws and receiving $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.

This week, I’ve been reading about nuclear radiation and F1 brains and phone scammers, watching about 10 minutes of Madden before bailing, playing a lot of Madden NFL instead, learning my way around Instagram Edits on the Mac, trying the 12-3-30 workout while watching Mission: Impossible movies in half-hour increments, getting my new Apple HomeView up and running (still don’t know why I bought one…), and dreaming up stuff to do with the Flipper One.

You may not know Tom Hovey, but I can practically guarantee you’ve seen his work. That’s because, in addition to many other cool projects, Tom’s also the artist behind those illustrated graphics of everyone’s bakes on The Great British Baking Show. His unique style has been all over that show, and my TV screen, for many years.

I found Tom’s work recently on Threads, when he went massively viral after debunking the idea that all those food drawings are AI with a video to prove how he does it. He’s been working with digital tools for a decade, he said, “but never ever AI.”

I asked Tom to share his homescreen with us to see how he might use his phone for his work, and also to see if I might learn any good GBBS spoilers. (Alas, none.) Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:

The wallpaper: A sunrise photo of the Swan River, where I run most mornings in Perth Western Australia. We moved here permanently 6 months ago.

The apps: Apple Podcasts, Brick, Sonos, Strava, SoundCloud, Photos, Google, Google Maps, iNaturalist, Google Calendar, Chrome, NYT Games, Gmail, WhatsApp, Spotify, Discord.

Like many people I’m addicted to my phone, so bricking my phone when I get home from the studio has been amazing. I’m obsessed with running, so Strava and Runna are used every day for training and logging my runs but also hyping up my running pals.

Six apps for my kids’ primary school is too many apps.

I have weather apps but it’s kinda unnecessary now we live in Australia, because it’s either hot or really hot!

iNaturalist is my newest app and I love it. It’s for documenting nature — flora and fauna. As I’m in a new country, I’m enjoying discovering all the native flowers and plants I find on runs. I’ve also recently done some trial runs in Perth Hills, where I’ve run into tons of wild kangaroos and snakes. So fun! My kids also love bugs and birds, so learning all about them is cool. Also when you add your photos of nature, it geotags them and sends the details to some scientists who can understand the areas you are documenting.

#250. Tesla's assisted driving system gets the green light for rollout in Italy

Tesla’s self-driving tech is awaiting another major vote from the European Union before the end of the year.

Italy's Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport has granted provisional approval for Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised), which has been rebranded to Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe. The Tesla Europe account on X confirmed in a post that it's been approved in Italy, with the rollout beginning soon. It also showed off footage of Tesla Assisted Driving operating near The Coliseum and on Italian roads. Italy's minister of infrastucture and transport, Matteo Salvini, also posted on X that Tesla's driver assistance system has been given the green light after a "timely technical feasibility review."

Italy's approval notches another regulatory milestone for Tesla since the country decided to preempt the European Union's expected vote on its driver assistance system slated for later this year. Tesla is still awaiting decisions from other major European Union countries, including Germany and France, which is currently in the process of testing Tesla Assisted Driving.

Tesla's self-driving tech first made its debut in Europe, thanks to the Dutch regulatory authority's provisional approval in April. Since then, several smaller European countries have followed suit, including Denmark, Belgium and Czechia.
